subject: Dedicated cluster options for SummitHealth — next steps
messages:
From: Laura Bennett <laura.bennett@redwood.ai>
To: Elaine Jones <elaine.jones@summithealth.com>
Cc: Tim Clarkson <tim@cloudadvisor.io>
Date: Fri, 02 Apr 2027 09:12:00 -0700
Subject: Dedicated cluster options for SummitHealth — next steps

Hi Elaine,

Great to meet you yesterday — thanks for walking through SummitHealth's peak inference profile. Per our conversation, I've pulled together three practical reservation options that balance latency SLOs, cost predictability, and a phased ramp to match your expected growth. I've attached a short one-pager (SummitHealth_Dedicated_Options_v2.pdf) and a simple cost workbook (SH_cost_model_burn_rate.xlsx).

Quick summary (high level):
- Option A — Conservative starter: 8x A100-equivalent GPUs, 1-month warm-up, autoscaling to 12 during peak (recommended if you want minimal upfront spend).
- Option B — Phased commit (recommended): commit to 32 GPUs over 12 months with a 3-month ramp (8 -> 16 -> 32); includes a 10% reserved discount and a burst pool for traffic spikes.
- Option C — Aggressive scale: 64 GPUs committed with a 30% discount, immediate capacity for large throughput (best for aggressive product launches).

Two notes on terms: minimum sustained throughput clauses (min GPUs) and early termination credits are included in the attached PDF; the cost workbook shows expected burn-rate by month for each option.

Ask: can you confirm which of these three you want us to model into an SOW/PO? If helpful, Ben and I can join a 30-min follow-up to walk the numbers with procurement.

Thanks,

—
Laura Bennett
Senior Account Executive | Redwood Inference
laura.bennett@redwood.ai | +1 415-555-0123

Attachments: SummitHealth_Dedicated_Options_v2.pdf (PDF, 3 pages), SH_cost_model_burn_rate.xlsx (Excel)

Laura —

Thanks for the clear options and the workbook. A couple quick clarifying questions before we loop in procurement:
1) For Option B, what do you define as the minimum sustained GPU obligation during the 3-month ramp? Is billing prorated daily or monthly?
2) How does the burst pool work if we exceed committed capacity for monitored peaks? Any hard overage caps?
3) Can you show an alternate phasing that starts at 12 GPUs instead of 8 — our initial peak prediction is a bit higher in April/May.

Also, procurement will want a simple monthly forecast they can attach to the PO. If you can send the monthly burn for a 12-month ramp with the 12->16->32 phasing, that will speed approvals.

Best,

Laura / Rishi —

Sketching responses to Elaine's questions. Key points to include in procurement-ready forecast:
- Billing cadence: monthly invoices with daily pro-rata used for mid-month scale events; we can anchor the PO to the month but credit prorated days for ramp steps.
- Min sustained: for Option B (3-mo ramp) we recommend a minimum billing floor equal to 75% of the committed GPUs at each ramp phase (so when they step from 8->16, the min is 12 until full 16 is reached). This protects cluster packing and yields predictable unit economics.
- Burst pool: 20% of committed capacity reserved as ephemeral burst for free; anything beyond will be billed at on-demand rate (we can cap overage to 40% of committed in the contract).

I've updated the cost workbook with a 12-start phasing as Elaine requested and included two burn-rate lines (with/without burst). See attached: SH_cost_model_burn_rate.xlsx (updated).

I recommend we present Option B with the 12->16->32 phased start as the recommended path — it reduces early overage risk and keeps Total Cost of Ownership reasonable. Laura, want to take this to procurement next week? I'll join.

—
Ben Carter
Enterprise Solutions | Redwood Inference

Elaine / Procurement team —

Thanks for the requests. Per Ben's analysis I've attached a concise option set tailored to your ask (SummitHealth_Dedicated_Options_v2.pdf) and an updated monthly forecast that starts at 12 GPUs. Highlights below: 

Recommended: Modified Option B (phased commit) — 12 -> 16 -> 32 over months 1, 4, and 9 respectively.
- Minimum sustained obligation: 75% of phase cap enforced by monthly billing; example: month 2 min = 0.75 * 12 = 9 (we'll round to nearest GPU for billing).
- Billing cadence: monthly invoice; partial-month prorate when phase changes occur mid-invoice.
- Burst handling: ephemeral burst up to 20% of committed capacity is included; overage above that billed at on-demand per-GPU rates and capped at 40% for any billing period.
- Early termination: scaled credit schedule (see PDF) to avoid a cliff hit.

Why we recommend this: it gives you room to validate load without paying for a full 32 immediately, keeps early burn predictable for Finance, and preserves capacity for sustained production traffic by the end of year.

Next steps: If procurement is comfortable with the min-floor and burst rules, we can draft the SOW and a PO-ready one-page forecast. Ben and I are available Wed/Thu next week for a 30-min call with procurement.

Thanks,

—
Laura Bennett
